Corroborated by Elugbe, Ben Ohiomamhe. 1989. Comparative Edoid: Phonology and Lexicon (Delta Series 6). Port Harcourt: University of Port Harcourt Press.
catalog_locator: Elugbe 1973, Uhami chapter (pp. 266-276), sec. 6 'Tone', p. 275 and fn. 1 (header 'Phonology: Uhami 275'). Elugbe 1989, sec. 4.18.8 'Tone', p. 97.
catalog_quote: 6. Tone [fn. 1] Two levels of tone are clearly distinctive in Uhami: high and low. High contrasts with low in the following minimal pair: /akɔ/ [_ _] 'tooth, teeth' (LL) /ákɔ/ [- _] 'day' (HL) A third level occurs in Uhami but it is not clear whether this third level should be analysed as a third significant (mid) tone or as a downstep. The latter analysis is tentatively adopted here for two reasons: (i) only two levels occur on lexical items (with the exception of /ɔ́dɛ̄/ [‾ -] 'hunter' (which is a borrowing from Yoruba (cf. Yoruba: ọdẹ 'hunter')) where a third level, neither low nor high occurs). (ii) the occurrence of the following sequences: (a) /mí ꜝ dɛ́/ [‾ -] 'I will buy' (b) /ó kɔnɔ́/ [‾ _ -] 'he will fight' Note the non-automatic downstep (a) and the apparently ... [fn. 1] My informants were very inconsistent with tone and this analysis must be taken as very tentative. Indeed, for the same reason, the completive phrase will not be discussed here, especially as they were more inconsistent with nouns than with verb phrases. (1973: 275) || 4.18.8. Tone Within the scope of the limited data at my disposal, high and low tones were found to be distinctive. A third mid level was also identified but it will probably be analysed as a downstep. Elugbe (1973) gives an example that suggests there may be downdrift in Uhami but makes the point that his informants were inconsistent with tone. (1989: 97)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Uhami is described as a tone language with two distinctive levels, high and low, plus a tentatively analysed downstep (third level); both descriptions are explicitly based on limited, inconsistent data. Neither source mentions stress or accent anywhere, so no rule for stress placement can be stated. A newer, login-walled study (Tunde 2024) claims four tones (H, M, L, falling) per its abstract, again with no mention of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone only: a third (mid) level appears in the Yoruba loan /ɔ́dɛ̄/ 'hunter' and in downstep sequences; a LMH sequence [ù dɔ̄ dé] 'you bought a house' is discussed as inconclusive evidence for a mid tone (1973: 275-276).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern lexical items (nouns, verbs) and short verb phrases; the completive phrase was left undescribed because of informant inconsistency (1973: 275 fn. 1). Stems are mostly monosyllabic (1989: 97).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Uhami as spoken in the two Ishuas (Isua-Akoko), Oyara and probably Shosan, Ondo State (Elugbe 1989: 7; informant P. A. Longe); Tunde 2024/2025 use the endonym Ùhànmì for the same Isua-Akoko speech form (Glottolog language_note 'Ùhànmì = Uhami [uha]'). No dialect split is described; all statements refer to uham1238 itself.

sources.citation: Olaogun, Simeon & Oluwaseun Oyelade. 2025. Negation, Tense and Aspect in North-Western Edoid. Beyond Babel: BU Journal of Language, Literature and Humanities 9(1): 370-381. Zenodo deposit doi:10.5281/zenodo.17129287.
sources.note: Zenodo abstract (read) is morphosyntactic: 'while habitual aspect in Proto Òssé, especially Ìsùà, is inflected for negation, Àbèsàbèsì employs a non-inflectional strategy.. negative markers typically precede the verb phrase (VP) in other Northwestern Edoid languages'. No tone word in the abstract. Because tense in Ùhànmì is marked by grammatical tone (Tunde & Ridwan 2024, held), the Isua negation/aspect paradigms in this paper very likely carry tone-marked clauses and may remark on tonal inflection, but that is unverified. Open 394 KB PDF not downloaded: tone statement already listed here.
